name: Holy Roman Empire
summary: The Holy Roman Empire was a composite and elective political structure. Imperial dignity, Roman royalty and the governments of their principalities were related but different positions; an emperor did not rule every feud as if it were his own hereditary domain.
notes: The elements highlighted throughout its history; its membership and autonomy varied. It does not imply hereditary domination of the emperor.

Consort of the Estuardo dynasty. Their life is linked to Bohemia, Palatinate.

The elector of the Palatinate and, during the winter of 1619–1620, king of Bohemia. His acceptance of the Bohemian crown turned a constitutional crisis into one of the triggers of the Thirty Years' War.
Consort of the Habsburg dynasty. Their life is linked to Bohemia, Holy Roman Empire, Spain.

personas.nombre: Ferdinand III of the Holy Roman Empire
personas.resumen: Emperor during the final phase of the Thirty Years' War. Participated in the negotiation of the political order that culminated in the Peace of Westphalia of 1648.
The eldest son of Emperor Ferdinand III, crowned King of Bohemia and Hungary and elected King of Romans in 1653. He died of smallpox in 1654 without succeeding his father.
Consort of the Habsburg dynasty. Their life is linked to Spain, Austria.
Consort of the Habsburg dynasty. Their life is linked to Spain, Holy Roman Empire, Bohemia.

personas.nombre: Leopold I of the Holy Roman Empire
personas.resumen: Emperor Habsburg for almost half a century. His reign was marked by wars against Louis XIV and by the great confrontation with the Ottoman Empire culminated in Vienna in 1683.
Consort of the Habsburg dynasty. Their life is linked to Austria, Bavaria.
Otto de Wittelsbach received the Bavarian Duchy of Frederick Barbarossa in 1180, after the fall of Henry the Lion. His house ruled Bavaria until 1918.
Consort of the Loon Dynasty. Their life is linked to Bavaria.
Duke of Bavaria, 1183–1231. Duke of the Wittelsbach dynasty.
Consort of the Přemysl dynasty. Their life is linked to Bohemia, Bavaria.
Otto the Illustrian, Duke of Bavaria, joined his house the Palatinate of the Rhine for his marriage to Inés del Palatinate. He supported the Staufen in front of the papacy.
Consort of the Welf dynasty. Their life is linked to Bavaria, Palatinate.
Duke of Bavaria, 1290–1296 (branch). Duke of the Wittelsbach dynasty.
Consort of the Piast dynasty. Their life is linked to Bavaria.
Duke of Bavaria, 1290–1310 (branch). Duke of the Wittelsbach dynasty.
Consort of the Luxembourg dynasty. Their life is linked to Bohemia, Bavaria.
Duke of Bavaria, 1312–1339 (branch). Duke of the Wittelsbach dynasty.
Duke of Bavaria, 1312–1334 (branch). Duke of the Wittelsbach dynasty.
Consort of the Wittelsbach dynasty. Their life is linked to Bavaria.
Duke of Bavaria, 1339–1340 (branch). Duke of the Wittelsbach dynasty.
Countess of the Gorizia dynasty. Her trajectory is linked to Tyrol, Bavaria.
Duke of Bavaria, 1347–1361 (branch). Duke of the Wittelsbach dynasty.
Duke of Bavaria, 1347–1351 (branch). Duke of the Wittelsbach dynasty.
Consort of the Luxembourg dynasty. Their life is linked to Bohemia, Bavaria.
Duke of Bavaria, 1347–1351 (branch). Duke of the Wittelsbach dynasty.
Consort of the Plantagenet-Lancaster dynasty. Their life is linked to Bavaria, England.
Duke of Bavaria-Straubing and Count of Hainaut, Holland and Zealand by inheritance from their mother. Their mental illness forced their brother Albert to rule as regent since 1358.
Consort of the Piast dynasty. Their life is linked to Bavaria.
Duke of Bavaria-Straubing and, by his mother Margaret, ruler of Hainaut, Holland and Zeeland. He was regent by his brother William I and Count to his death in 1389.
Duke of Bavaria, 1389–1397 (branch). Duke of the Wittelsbach dynasty.
Duke of Bavaria, 1361–1363 (branch). Duke of the Wittelsbach dynasty.
Consort of the Visconti dynasty. Their life is linked to Bavaria, Milan.
Duke of Bavaria, 1375–1393 (branch). Duke of the Wittelsbach dynasty.
Consort of the Gorizia dynasty. Their life is linked to Bavaria.
Duke of Bavaria, 1375–1397 (branch). Duke of the Wittelsbach dynasty.
Consort of the Habsburg dynasty. Their life is linked to Austria, Bavaria.
Duke of Bavaria, 1393–1450 (branch). Duke of the Wittelsbach dynasty.
Consort of the Visconti dynasty. Their life is linked to Bavaria, Milan.
Duke of Bavaria, 1397–1438 (branch). Duke of the Wittelsbach dynasty.
Consort of the La Marck dynasty. Their life is linked to Bavaria.
Duke of Bavaria, 1397–1435 (branch). Duke of the Wittelsbach dynasty.
Consort of the Valois-Burgundy dynasty. Their life is linked to Burgundy, Bavaria.
Duke of Bavaria-Straubing and Count of Hainaut, Holland and Zeeland from 1404. His daughter Jacqueline inherited those counties, which were later contested by Philip the Good of Burgundy.
Consort of the Bourbon dynasty. Their life is linked to Bavaria.
Duke of Bavaria, 1413–1443 (branch). Duke of the Wittelsbach dynasty.
Duchess of Luxembourg, 1411–1443. Duchess of the Luxembourg dynasty.
Duke of Bavaria, 1417–1425 (branch). Duke of the Wittelsbach dynasty.
Consort of the Welf dynasty. Their life is linked to Bavaria.
Duke of Bavaria-Munich between 1438 and 1460. His union with Agnes Bernauer ended when his father, Duke Ernesto, drowned her on the Danube in 1435.
Duke of Bavaria, 1443–1445 (branch). Duke of the Wittelsbach dynasty.
Consort of the Wettin dynasty. Their life is linked to Bavaria, Saxony.
Duke of Bavaria, 1450–1479 (branch). Duke of the Wittelsbach dynasty.
Duke of Bavaria, 1460–1463 (branch). Duke of the Wittelsbach dynasty.
Duke of Bavaria-Munich between 1460 and 1467, when he abdicated in his brother Albert IV. In 1468 he laid the first stone of the Munich Frauenkirche.
Consort of the Jagelón dynasty. Their life is linked to Poland, Bavaria.
Duke of Bavaria, 1479–1503 (branch). Duke of the Wittelsbach dynasty.
Consort of the Habsburg dynasty. Their life is linked to Austria, Bavaria.
Albert IV the Wise reunited Bavaria after the succession war of Landshut (1503–1505) and in 1506 established the birthright to avoid new partitions.
Consort of the Zähringen dynasty. Their life is linked to Bavaria.
Duke of Bavaria between 1508 and 1550, initially in dispute with his brother Louis X. In 1516 he promulgated with him the decree on the purity of beer.
Duke of Bavaria, 1516–1545 (co-ruler). Duke of the Wittelsbach dynasty.
Consort of the Habsburg dynasty. Their life is linked to Austria, Bavaria.

Duke of Bavaria since 1597 and head of the Catholic League. After the victory of the White Mountain (1620) he received the electoral dignity of Frederick V of the Palatinate (1623) and the High Palatinate.
Consort of the Leuchtenberg dynasty. Their life is linked to Bavaria.
Duke of Bavaria, 1646–1666 (branch). Duke of the Wittelsbach dynasty.
Consort of the Savoy dynasty. Their life is linked to Bavaria, Savoy.
Elector of Bavaria, 1651–1679. Elector of the Wittelsbach dynasty.
Duke of Bavaria, 1666–1705 (branch). Duke of the Wittelsbach dynasty.
Consort of the Sobieski dynasty. Their life is linked to Bavaria, Poland.
Elector of Bavaria, 1679–1726. Elector of the Wittelsbach dynasty.
Condotiero of the Hawkwood Dynasty. Their life is linked to Florence, Milan, Pontifical States.
Condotiero of the Piccinino dynasty. Their life is linked to Milan, Florence.
Condotiero of the Piccinino dynasty. Their life is linked to Milan, Naples.
Condotiero of the Piccinino dynasty. Their life is linked to Milan, Naples.
Condotiero of the Bussone dynasty. Their life is linked to Milan.

Condotiero of the nobility of Bergamo, Bartolomeo Colleoni fought for various Italian powers before consolidating himself as captain general of Venice in 1454. His fortune held possessions, foundations and artistic commissions in the territory of Bergamasco. He died in 1475.
Marquis of the Ávalos dynasty. Their life is linked to Naples, Milan.
Condotiero of the Gonzaga dynasty. Their life is linked to Mantua, Milan.
Condotiero of the Trivulzio dynasty. Their life is linked to Milan, France.
Consort of the Wittelsbach dynasty. Their life is linked to France, Bavaria.
Duke of Savoy who took advantage of the Spanish War of Succession to raise the rank of his house. He first became king of Sicily and then king of Sardinia.
Consort of the Bourbon-Orleans dynasty. Their life is linked to France, Savoy.
Consort of the Savoy dynasty. Their life is linked to France, Savoy.
Consort of the Wettin dynasty. Their life is linked to France, Saxony.
Daughter of Mary Theresa of Austria and Queen of France for her marriage to Louis XVI. In prison during the Revolution, she was guillotined in 1793.
Last Habsburg king of Spain. His lack of descent turned his succession into a European question and, after his death, triggered the Spanish War of Succession.
Consort of the Savoy dynasty. Their life is linked to Spain, Savoy.

First Bourbon king of Spain. The War of Succession made him lose Milan, Naples and Sardinia; he recovered the latter briefly between 1717 and 1720. His peninsular and Italian domains followed different paths.
Consort of the Wettin dynasty. Their life is linked to Spain, Saxony.
Artist, engineer and researcher of the Renaissance. He worked for different Italian courts and ended his days in France under the protection of Francis I.
Governor of the Amboise dynasty. Their life is linked to France, Milan.
Artist of the Melzi dynasty. Their life is linked to Milan, France.
Consort of the Celje dynasty. Their life is linked to Hungary, Bohemia, Holy Roman Empire.
Noble of the Sforza dynasty. Their life is linked to Milan.
Consort of the Habsburg dynasty. Their life is linked to the Holy Roman Empire, Austria.
Consort of the Wittelsbach dynasty. Their life is linked to the Holy Roman Empire, Palatinate.

personas.nombre: Joseph I of the Holy Roman Empire
personas.resumen: Emperor Habsburg during the Spanish War of Succession. He continued the policy of his father Leopold I and supported the candidacy of his brother Charles to the Spanish throne.
Consort of the Welf dynasty. Their life is linked to the Holy Roman Empire.

personas.nombre: Charles VI of the Holy Roman Empire
personas.resumen: Emperor Habsburg and rival of Philip V in the War of Succession. His house ruled Milan, Naples and Sardinia on different dates; he traded Sardinia for Sicily in 1720. The Pragmatic Sanction sought to secure his inheritance to Mary Theresa.
Consort of the Welf Dynasty. Their life is linked to the Holy Roman Empire, Austria.
Consort of the Habsburg dynasty. Their life is linked to Bavaria, Holy Roman Empire, Austria.

personas.nombre: Charles VII of the Holy Roman Empire
personas.resumen: The Bavarian Elector elected emperor during the Austrian War of Succession. His election broke for a few years the long continuity of the Habsburgs in imperial dignity.
Elector of Bavaria, 1745–1777. Elector of the Wittelsbach dynasty.
Consort of the Wittelsbach dynasty. Their life is linked to Palatinate, Orleans, France.
Consort of the Bourbon-Orleans dynasty, their life is linked to Orleans, Lorraine.
He recovered the duchy of Lorraine in 1697 for the peace of Ryswick and ruled it until 1729. He was the father of Francisco Esteban, husband of Mary Theresa and emperor.

personas.nombre: Francis I Stephen of the Holy Roman Empire
personas.resumen: Duke of Lorraine and then Grand Duke of Tuscany, he became emperor by his marriage to Mary Theresa. His union founded the house of Habsburg-Lorraine.

Sovereign of the hereditary domains of the Habsburgs and one of the great figures of the eighteenth century. He defended his heritage in the Austrian War of Succession and promoted important administrative reforms.

personas.nombre: Joseph II of the Holy Roman Empire
personas.resumen: Emperor Habsburg associated with enlightened despotism. He tried to thoroughly modernize the administration, the Church and society of his territories through a very ambitious reform program.
Consort of the Bourbon dynasty. Their life is linked to Spain, Tuscany, Holy Roman Empire.

personas.nombre: Leopold II of the Holy Roman Empire
personas.resumen: Emperor Habsburg of brief reign, succeeded after governing Tuscany. He moderated several reforms of Joseph II and faced the expansion of the French Revolution in Europe.

personas.nombre: Francis II of the Holy Roman Empire
personas.resumen: The last emperor of the Holy Roman Empire and first emperor of Austria since 1804. He fought against revolutionary and Napoleonic France, dissolved the Empire in 1806 and married his daughter Mary Louise to Napoleon.
Dutch humanist and one of the great intellectual figures of the European Renaissance. He defended a Christian reform based on education and philology without breaking with Rome.
German theologian whose criticism of indulgences triggered the Protestant Reformation. His break with Rome transformed the religion, politics and culture of Europe.
Fraile, their life is linked to the Holy Roman Empire.
Their life is linked to the Holy Roman Empire, Saxony.
His path is linked to the Holy Roman Empire.
His path is linked to the Holy Roman Empire.
Cardinal, their life is linked to Milan, the Papal States.
Elector of Saxony since 1464. In the partition of Leipzig (1485) with his brother Alberto founded the Wettin Ernestine line, which preserved electoral dignity until 1547.
Consort of the Wittelsbach dynasty. Their life is linked to Bavaria, Saxony.
Frederick the Wise, Elector of Saxony since 1486. He founded Wittenberg University (1502) and protected Martin Luther, who had him hide in the castle of Wartburg after the Diet of Worms (1521).
John the Constant, Elector of Saxony between 1525 and 1532. He organized a Lutheran territorial church, presented the Augsburg Confession (1530) and was one of the founders of the Eshmachalda League.
Consort of the Mecklenburg dynasty. Their life is linked to Saxony.

Juan Federico el Magnanimo, Elector of Saxony since 1532 and head of the Eshmachalda League. Defeated and captured by Carlos V in Mühlberg (1547), lost electoral dignity in favor of his cousin Mauricio.

Landgrave of Hesse and one of the most important Protestant princes of the Reformation. After his death, the territory was divided among his sons and gave rise to branches such as Hesse-Kassel and Hesse-Darmstadt.
Noble of the Cusani dynasty. Their life is linked to Milan.

The daughter of Leopold VI of Babenberg and Theodora, Constance of Austria married in 1234 Henry III, Margrave of Misnia. His marriage linked the Babenbergs to the Wettin. He was the mother of Albert and Dietrich; he died in 1243, before the Austrian successor crisis of 1246.
Consort of the Wittelsbach dynasty. Their life is linked to Bavaria, Meißen.
Margrave of Meissen who in 1423 received from Emperor Segismund the duchy and electorate of Saxony, initiating the Wettin government in the electorate.
Consort of the Welf dynasty. Their life is linked to Saxony.
Elector of Saxony since 1428, from the house of Wettin. He ruled with his brother Guillermo, with whom he fought the fratricidal Saxon war; his sons Ernesto and Alberto later divided the domains.
Consort of the Piast dynasty. Their life is linked to Austria, Mazovia.
Consort of the Habsburg dynasty. Their life is linked to Austria, Saxony.
Alberto el Animoso founded the Wettin's pool line for the partition of Leipzig (1485) with his brother Ernesto. He served Maximilian I as commander and governor of Friesland.
Consort of the Poděbrady dynasty. Their life is linked to Bohemia, Saxony.
George the Barbud, Duke of the Albertine Saxony since 1500 and defender of Catholicism against Luther. He organized the Leipzig dispute of 1519 between Luther and Johann Eck.
Consort of the Jagelón dynasty. Their life is linked to Poland, Lithuania, Saxony.
Consort of the Wettin dynasty. Their life is linked to Saxony, Hesse.
Henry the Pious succeeded his brother George in 1539 in the Albertina Saxony and introduced the Lutheran Reformation there.
Consort of the Mecklenburg dynasty. Their life is linked to Saxony.

Duke of Saxony, allied himself with Charles V against the Eshmachalda League and obtained in 1547 the electoral dignity of his cousin. In 1552 he turned against the emperor and forced peace in Passau; he died in the Battle of Sievershausen (1553).
Consort of the Hessen dynasty. Their life is linked to Hesse, Saxony.
Brother of Mauritius, Elector of Saxony since 1553. He defended Orthodox Lutheranism, reorganized the administration of the electorate and gathered in Dresden a chamber of art and wonders.
Consort of the Oldenburg Dynasty. Their life is linked to Denmark, Saxony.
Elector of Saxony between 1586 and 1591. With his Chancellor Nikolaus Krell he favored an approach to Calvinism that was thrown away after his death.
Consort of the Hohenzollern dynasty. Their life is linked to Brandenburg, Saxony.
Elector of Saxony, 1591–1611. Elector of the Wettin dynasty.
Elector of Saxony between 1611 and 1656. In the Thirty Years' War he oscillated between the emperor and Sweden; for the peace of Prague (1635) he definitely obtained Lusatius.
Consort of the Hohenzollern dynasty. Their life is linked to Prussia, Saxony.
Elector of Saxony, 1656–1680. Elector of the Wettin dynasty.
Consort of the Hohenzollern dynasty. Their life is linked to Saxony.
Elector of Saxony between 1680 and 1691. He created a permanent army and participated with his troops in the Vienna relief of 1683.
Consort of the Oldenburg Dynasty. Their life is linked to Denmark, Saxony.
Elector of Saxony, 1691–1694. Elector of the Wettin dynasty.
Elector of Saxony elected king of Poland, known for his enormous physical strength and ambitious dynastic politics. His participation in the Great War of the North weakened the Commonwealth.
Consort of the Hohenzollern dynasty. Their life is linked to Saxony.
French Marshal of the Wettin Dynasty. Their life is linked to Saxony, France.
Elector of Saxony and king of Poland during a period of growing political paralysis of the Commonwealth. His reign reinforced the dynastic connection between Dresden and Warsaw.
Consort of the Habsburg dynasty. Their life is linked to Austria, Saxony, Poland.
Elector of Saxony, 1763–1763. Elector of the Wettin dynasty.
Consort of the Wittelsbach dynasty. Their life is linked to Bavaria, Saxony.
Regent of Saxony, 1763–1768. Prince of the Wettin Dynasty.
Last elector and first king of Saxony (1806). Allied to Napoleon, he was also Duke of Warsaw since 1807; in 1815 he lost about half of his kingdom to Prussia.
Count Palatine of Palatinate, 1195–1214. Count Palatinate of the Welf dynasty.
Consort of the Hohenstaufen dynasty. Their life is linked to Palatinate.
He consolidated the Saudi domains on both sides of the Alps after a difficult minority. His offspring opened paths to the English and Provencal courts and to the Italian lordships.
Consort of the Geneva Dynasty. Their life is linked to Savoy, Geneva.
He succeeded Thomas I and had to negotiate with his brothers the distribution of family rights. His Italian policy brought him closer to Frederick II.
Consort of the Burgundy dynasty. Their life is linked to Savoy, Burgundy.
Consort of the Baux dynasty. Their life is linked to Savoy, Provence.
Count of Savoy, 1253–1263. Count of Savoy dynasty.

Before inheriting the county, he developed an important career in England and gathered his own domains around Lake Leman. His government reinforced controls over Castilians, Revenues and Administration.
He abandoned his ecclesiastical career before succeeding his brother Peter II. Without his own offspring, he had to prepare an inheritance in which the sons and grandchildren of Thomas II competed.
Brother of Amadeus IV, he received rights in Piedmont and ruled Flanders for his marriage to Joan. He was not the successor of his father in Savoy County.
Consort of the Fieschi dynasty. Their life is linked to Piedmont, Savoy.

Son of Thomas II, he entered the county after the death of his uncle Philip I. His position was consolidated by agreements with other branches of the family, which retained their own rights. Edward and Aimon succeeded in Savoy; by their marriages, the count also linked with Bâgé and Brabant.
Consort of the Bâgé dynasty. Their life is linked to Savoy.
Count of Savoy, 1323–1329. Count of Savoy dynasty.

Amadeus V's youngest son, inherited after his brother Edward, whose daughter also defended inheritance rights. His marriage to Yolanda de Montferrat united the Savoy with the new Italian branch of the Paleologists.
Daughter of Theodore I of Montferrat, he married Aimon of Savoy. His ancestry was linked to Emperor Andronic II and to the Alleramic heiress Yolanda, named Irene in Byzantium.

Known as the Green Count, he belongs to the generation that reinforced Savoy’s political and military projection. He was the son of Aimon and Yolanda of Montferrat, so his ancestry brings together Savoy and Palaeologists.
Consort of the Bourbon dynasty. Their life is linked to Bourbon, Savoy.

The Red Count succeeded his father Amadeus VI and maintained the relationship with the French monarchy. He married Bona de Berry and was the father of Amadeus VIII. His early death left a child heir and opened a struggle for regency between the mother and grandmother of the new Count.
Consort of the Valois dynasty. Their life is linked to France, Savoy.
He inherited as a child and became the first Duke of Savoy in 1416. The elevation of rank did not create a new dynasty.
Consort of the Valois-Burgundy dynasty. Their life is linked to Burgundy, Savoy.
The son of Amadeus VIII and Mary of Burgundy, he assumed government functions before becoming Duke. His marriage to Anna of Lusignan linked Savoy to Cyprus.

Daughter of King Janus of Cyprus, he married Louis of Savoy and brought to the Alpine court a direct connection with the Lusignans. His numerous offspring linked with France, Milan and the Cypriot succession itself.
Duke of Savoy since 1465, fragile health due to epilepsy. His wife Yolanda of France ruled in practice. He was beatified by his piety.
Consort of the Valois dynasty. Their life is linked to France, Savoy.
Duke of Savoy, 1472–1482. Duke of Savoy Dynasty.

He inherited the duchy of his brother Filiberto I. His marriage to Blanca de Montferrat reinforced Savoy's expectations of the Palaeologists' heritage, while the intervention in Saluzzo confronted him with French interests.

The son of Louis and Anna of Cyprus, he came to the duchy when the male offspring of his brother Amadeus IX were extinguished. His brief government preceded those of his sons Filiberto II and Charles III, born of different marriages.
Consort of the Bourbon dynasty. Their life is linked to Bourbon, Savoy.
Consort of the Brose dynasty, their life is linked to Savoy.
He inherited from his father Philip II and married Margaret of Austria. The link brought Savoy closer to the Habsburgs and the Netherlands.
Duke of Savoy between 1504 and 1553. In 1536 France occupied almost all its states and Geneva consolidated its independence; their son Manuel Filiberto recovered them in 1559.
Consort of the Avis dynasty. Their life is linked to Portugal, Savoy.

He inherited a duchy occupied largely by other powers. His service to Charles V and Philip II, and especially the victory of San Quintin, contributed to the territorial recovery agreed at Cateau-Cambresis.
Consort of the Valois-Angulema dynasty. Their life is linked to France, Savoy.
The son of Manuel Filiberto, he ruled in a scenario dominated by rivalries between France and the Hispanic monarchy. His marriage to Catherine Micaela connected him to Philip II.

The daughter of Philip II and Isabel of Valois, he married Charles Manuel I of Savoy. His marriage placed the descendants of the Duke within the family network of the Habsburgs and the Valois. Among his sons were Victor Amadeus I and Thomas Francis, for whom he continued the branch of Carignano.

The youngest son of Carlos Manuel I and Catalina Micaela, he began the Savoy-Carignano branch. He married Maria de Borbón-Soissons and participated in the disputes against the regency of Cristina de France.
Princess of Carignano of the Bourbon-Condé dynasty. Her trajectory is linked to France, Savoy.

Son of Thomas Francis of Savoy-Carignano, he inherited the county of Soissons for his mother and served as general in the armies of Louis XIV. He married Olympia Mancini, niece of Mazarino, and was the father of Prince Eugene.

Prince of Savoy-Carignanus's house raised in the court of Louis XIV, passed in 1683 to the Habsburgs and became the great general of the Empire. He defeated the Ottomans in Zenta (1697) and Belgrade (1717) and, together with Marlborough, to France in Blenheim, Oudenarde and Malplaquet during the Spanish War of Succession.
Duke of Savoy, 1638–1675. Duke of Savoy Dynasty.
Consort of the Savoy-Nemours dynasty. Their life is linked to Savoy, France.
King of Sardinia and Duke of Savoy who continued the territorial expansion of his dynasty in northern Italy. He actively participated in the great European wars of the eighteenth century.
Consort of the Hessen dynasty. Their life is linked to Hesse, Savoy.
King of Sardinia and Duke of Savoy since 1773. The war with revolutionary France cost Savoy and Nice, given over by the armistice of Cherasco in 1796.
Consort of the Bourbon dynasty. Their life is linked to Spain, Savoy.
King of Sardinia since 1796. French troops forced him to leave their continental states in 1798; he took refuge in Sardinia and abdicated in his brother Victor Manuel I in 1802.
Consort of the Bourbon dynasty. Their life is linked to France, Savoy.
King of Sardinia since 1802. He recovered Piedmont and Savoy in 1814 and obtained Genoa at the Congress of Vienna; abdicated in 1821 after the Piedmontese liberal revolution.
King of Sardinia between 1821 and 1831, brother of Victor Manuel I. He restored an absolutist government after the revolution of 1821 and was the last of the Savoy's main line.
The son of Thomas Francis and Mary of Bourbon-Soissons, continued the branch of Carignano. Her marriage to Angela Caterina of East added an Italian connection to the Savoyrd and Bourbon heritage.
Princess of Carignano of the East Dynasty. Her trajectory is linked to Modena, Savoy.
Prince of Carignano of the Savoy-Carignan dynasty. Their life is linked to Savoy, Piedmont.
Princess of Carignano of the Savoy dynasty. Her trajectory is linked to Savoy.
Prince of Carignano of the Savoy-Carignan dynasty. Their life is linked to Savoy, Piedmont.
Princess of Carignano of the Hessen dynasty. Her trajectory is linked to Hesse, Savoy.
Prince of Carignano of the Savoy-Carignan dynasty. Their life is linked to Savoy, Piedmont.
Princess of Carignano of the Lorraine dynasty. Her trajectory is linked to Lorraine, Savoy.
Prince of Carignano of the Savoy-Carignan dynasty. Their life is linked to Savoy, Piedmont.

personas.nombre: Charles of Saxony, Duke of Curlandia
personas.resumen: Duke of Curlandia, 1758–1763. Duke of the Wettin Dynasty.
Consort of the Krasiński dynasty. Their life is linked to Poland, Saxony.
Princess of Carignan of the Wettin Dynasty. Her trajectory is linked to Saxony, Savoy.
King of Sardinia since 1831, of the Savoy-Carignano branch. He granted the Statute of 1848 and declared war on Austria; defeated in Novara (1849), abdicated in Victor Manuel II.

Wife of King John and daughter of Wettin's house. Stockholm defended during the Swedish rebellion of 1501 and was imprisoned after the capitulation. She was the mother of Cristian II: her experience illustrates the fragility of the common government before the last attempt to preserve the union.
Consort of the Hohenzollern dynasty. Their life is linked to Brandenburg, Sweden.

Daughter of Charles IX and Mary of the Palatinate. Her marriage to Juan Casimiro of the Palatinate-Zweibrücken connected the Vasa with a branch of Wittelsbach. Her son Carlos X Gustavo succeeded Cristina of Sweden: the dynastic name change did not break the family continuity by female line.
Count Palatine of the Wittelsbach dynasty. Their life is linked to Palatinate, Sweden.
Consort of the Habsburg dynasty. Their life is linked to Austria, Tuscany.
Electora consort of the Medici dynasty. Their life is linked to Tuscany, Palatinate.
Elector Palatino since 1690, of the Newfoundburg branch of the Wittelsbach, known as Jan Wellem. From Düsseldorf he was a great patron and brother of several queens, including Mariana of Newburg.
Consort of the Wittelsbach dynasty. Their life is linked to Palatinate, Sweden.
Burgrave of Nuremberg, received from Sigismund the government of Brandenburg in 1415 and the investiture as Elector in 1417. He was the first Hohenzollern to head the electorate.
Consort of the Wittelsbach dynasty. Their life is linked to Bavaria, Brandenburg.
Frederick Iron Tooth, elector of Brandenburg between 1440 and 1470. He subjected the cities of Berlin and Cölln and recovered in 1455 the New Mark from the hands of the Teutonic Order.
The Brandenburg Elector between 1470 and 1486. By the Achillea Dispositio (1473) he fixed that the Brand of Brandenburg would pass undivided to a single heir.
Consort of the Baden Dynasty. Their life is linked to Brandenburg.
Consort of the Wettin dynasty. Their life is linked to Saxony, Brandenburg.
Margrave of Brandenburg, 1426–1440. Margrave of the Hohenzollern dynasty.

He married first Christopher of Bavaria and, after widowing, Cristian I. This marital continuity connected two different successor solutions for Denmark. He was the mother of John and Frederick I and defended his own patrimonial interests; his role is not reduced to being a link between two kings.
Elector of Brandenburg, 1486–1499. Elector of the Hohenzollern dynasty.
Consort of the Wettin Dynasty. Their life is linked to Thuringia, Brandenburg.
Elector of Brandenburg, 1499–1535. Elector of the Hohenzollern dynasty.
Consort of the Oldenburg Dynasty. Their life is linked to Denmark, Brandenburg.
Elector of Brandenburg, 1535–1571. Elector of the Hohenzollern dynasty.
Consort of the Wettin dynasty. Their life is linked to Saxony, Brandenburg.
Elector of Brandenburg, 1571–1598. Elector of the Hohenzollern dynasty.
Consort of the Piast dynasty. Their life is linked to Silesia, Brandenburg.
He took over the administration of the Duchy of Prussia in 1605 because of the illness of his duke, a step prior to the union of the two territories.
Consort of the Hohenzollern dynasty. Their life is linked to Brandenburg.
Consort of the Jagelón dynasty. Their life is linked to Poland, Brandenburg.
Consort of the Hohenzollern dynasty. Their life is linked to Prussia, Brandenburg.
Elector of Brandenburg since 1608. In 1613 he adopted Calvinism and in 1618 inherited the Duchy of Prussia, which united Brandenburg under the Hohenzollern.
Consort of the Nassau dynasty. Their life is linked to the Netherlands, Palatinate.
Elector of Palatinate, 1583–1610. Elector of the Wittelsbach dynasty.
Consort of the Wittelsbach dynasty. Their life is linked to Palatinate, Brandenburg.
Elector of Brandenburg and Duke of Prussia since 1619. During his rule Brandenburg suffered harshly the Thirty Years' War, occupied by Swedes and Imperials.
The Great Elector of Brandenburg (1640–1688) rebuilt his states after the Thirty Years' War, created a permanent army and gained full sovereignty over Prussia in 1657.
Consort of the Nassau dynasty. Their life is linked to the Netherlands, Brandenburg.
The Elector of Brandenburg who obtained the dignity of king in Prussia in 1701. His coronation raised the rank of the Hohenzollern and prepared the rise of the Prussian kingdom.
King of Prussia who built an austere administration and an exceptionally disciplined army. His state work provided Frederick the Great with a powerful military and fiscal machinery.
King of Prussia, military commander and enlightened monarch. His wars with Austria elevated Prussia to the rank of great European power.

He was the nephew and successor of Frederick II the Great, king of Prussia since 1786. He participated in the Polish divisions of 1793 and 1795 and in the first coalition against revolutionary France.
King of Prussia since 1797. After defeating Napoleon in Jena (1806) he supported the reforms of Stein and Hardenberg and participated in the coalition that defeated France in 1813–1815.
King of Prussia since 1861 and first German emperor since 1871. With Bismarck as Chancellor, the wars against Denmark, Austria and France culminated in the unification of Germany.
The voter of the Wittelsbach dynasty. Her trajectory is linked to Palatinate, Hannover.
Consort of the Hohenzollern dynasty. Their life is linked to Brandenburg, England.
Consort of the Wettin dynasty. Their life is linked to Saxony, England.
Consort of the Wettin dynasty. Their life is linked to Saxony, Netherlands.
Consort of the Hohenzollern dynasty. Their life is linked to Brandenburg, Denmark.
Consort of the Hohenzollern dynasty. Their life is linked to Brandenburg, Denmark.
Consort of the Hohenzollern dynasty. Their life is linked to Brandenburg, Denmark.
Consort of the Wettin dynasty. Their life is linked to Saxony, Holstein.
Consort of the Habsburg dynasty. Their life is linked to Austria, Poland, Lithuania.
King-elect of Poland on two occasions and father-in-law of Louis XV of France. After losing the crown he received Lorraine, where he developed a remarkable illustrated court.
Consort of the Pfirt dynasty. Their life is linked to Pfirt, Austria.
Consort of the Hohenzollern dynasty. Their life is linked to Nuremberg, Austria.
Consort of the Wittelsbach dynasty. Their life is linked to Bavaria, Austria.
Consort of the Ascania dynasty. Their life is linked to Saxony, Brandenburg.
Consort of the Brabant dynasty. Their life is linked to Brabant, Savoy.
Daughter of Amadeus V of Savoy and wife of Andronicus III Palaeologian. He was regent by his son John V during the civil war against John Cantacuceno (1341–1347).
Notary of the Medici dynasty of Milan. Their life is linked to Milan.
Noble of the Serbelloni dynasty. Their life is linked to Milan.
Consort of the Wittelsbach dynasty. Their life is linked to Bavaria, Thuringia.
The titular Duke of Lorraine, occupied by France, and Marshal in the service of Emperor Leopold I. He sent the imperial troops to the rescue of Vienna (1683) and the seizure of Buda (1686).
Archdukes of the Habsburg dynasty. Their life is linked to Austria, Lorraine.
Imperial commander who led the defence of Vienna during the Ottoman siege of 1683. His resistance allowed the city to be maintained until the arrival of the relief army.
Consort of the Wittelsbach dynasty. Their life is linked to Palatinate, Württemberg.
Consort of the Hohenzollern dynasty. Their life is linked to Brandenburg, Jülich, Berg.
Consort of the Habsburg dynasty. Their life is linked to Austria, Jülich, Cléveris.
Consort of the La Marck dynasty. Their life is linked to Cleves, Saxony.
Consort of the Lorraine dynasty. Their life is linked to Lorraine, Alençon.
Consort of the Wittelsbach dynasty. Their life is linked to Palatinate, Parma.

personas.nombre: Catherine of Brandenburg, Princess of Transylvania
personas.resumen: Elected successor to her husband Gabriel Bethlen, she ruled briefly in her own right. Her resignation in 1630 shows the limits that the estates and factions imposed on princely power; it was not just a consort.

The daughter of Bernabò Visconti, she married Peter II to strengthen relations between Milan and Cyprus. Her only daughter died a little. After widowing she returned to Italy; she should not be confused with Valentina Visconti, Duchess of Orleans.

personas.nombre: Louis of Savoy, King of Cyprus
personas.resumen: The son of Louis of Savoy and Anna of Cyprus, he married his cousin Carlota. His royal dignity came from that marriage and was then reduced to a pretense in exile. It should not be confused with his father, Duke of Savoy.

The son of Juan de Foix and Maria de Orleans, he was nephew of Louis XII and brother of Germana de Foix. He led French forces during the Italian wars and died in the Battle of Ravenna in 1512. His career brings together the Pyrenean connections of the Foix and military service to the French monarchy.

Erik’s sister from Pomerania. She married John of the Palatinate-Neumarkt, from the house of Wittelsbach. Her son Christopher was elected in the three Nordic kingdoms after Erik’s fall. Filiation shows family continuity, although Christopher’s access depended on separate choices.

Son of the king of Romans Rupert and member of the house of Wittelsbach. His marriage to Catherine of Pomerania linked his palatine branch with Erik of Pomerania. He was the father of Christopher of Bavaria, whose choice in the Scandinavian kingdoms extended that connection beyond the German territories.

The daughter of William VIII of Montferrat, he married Charles I of Savoy. After the death of the Duke he assumed the regency for his son Carlos Juan Amadeo and defended his authority before the relatives of the house.
The son of Charles I and Blanca de Montferrat, Savoy inherited before his first birthday. His mother exercised the regency.

personas.nombre: Joan of Savoy, Marquise of Montferrat
personas.resumen: Daughter of Amadeus VII and Bona de Berry, she married Juan James of Montferrat. She was the mother of William VIII, Bonifacio III and Isabel, wife of Ludovico I of Saluzzo.

He inherited the electoral dignity of his father Ruperto in 1410. The family division left separate palatinas branches; since 1435 a guardianship council exercised the government because of his illness.
The son of Louis III, he agreed to be a minor. A guardianship council administered the Kurpfalz until he personally assumed the government in 1442.
Brother of Louis IV, he assumed electoral dignity in 1449. His access opened a tutelage and a successor arrangement whose final beneficiary was his nephew Philip.
Nephew of Frederick I, succeeded in electoral dignity in 1476. His offspring continued the ruling line of the Kurpfalz during the first half of the 16th century.
The Palatinate's elector since 1508. His brother Frederick II succeeded him; none of these governments should be confused with the collateral branches of Pfalz-Neuburg.
Brother and successor of Louis V, he ruled the electoral Palatinate until 1556. Otto Henry followed him, coming from the Neuburg branch.
He ruled Pfalz-Neuburg with his brother Philip since 1522 and then alone. In 1556, palatine electoral dignity kept the two principalities separate; Neuburg gave to Wolfgang de Zweibrücken in 1557.
Since 1559, the Elector has promoted Calvinism in the Palatinate. His son Louis VI has changed confessional politics again.
He succeeded Frederick III in 1576 and returned to Lutheranism. His son Frederick IV was younger when he died in 1583; the government was under guardianship until 1592.

The son of Frederick V and Elizabeth Stuart, he was restored as the elector for the Peace of Westphalia in 1648. He recovered a reduced Palatinate: Bavaria preserved the Palatinate High and the old electoral dignity.
He succeeded his father Charles Louis in 1680. He died without an heir in 1685, so the electoral dignity passed to the Palatinate-Neuburg branch.

He inherited Jülich and Berg from Wolfgang Guillermo in 1653 and succeeded him at the electoral Palatinate in 1685. Coinciding in one person did not automatically merge the Renan ducats with the Kurpfalz.

personas.nombre: Charles III Philip of the Palatinate-Neoburg
personas.resumen: Duke of Palatinate-Neoburg, 1716–1742. Elector of the Wittelsbach dynasty.
Duke of Palatinate-Neoburg, 1742–1799. Elector of the Wittelsbach dynasty.
Bavarian Elector, 1799–1806. Voter of the Wittelsbach dynasty.

Duke of Styria and, since 1198, also of Austria, Leopold VI of Babenberg combined the expansion of his heritage with the support of monasteries and cities. He participated in the crusades and measured between Frederick II and the papacy. He died in St. German in 1230 and succeeded him his son Frederick.
Lord of Milan, 1339–1349 (co-ruler).
Lord of Milan, 1339–1354 (co-ruler).

Preacher and teacher of the University of Prague, he defended the reform of the Church and criticized the sale of indulgences. He was condemned for heresy and executed at the Council of Constance in 1415. His memory gave name to the Hussite movement.

He was the commander of the Hussite wars, and he was distinguished by the discipline of his troops and the use of fortified chariots. He led campaigns against the armies that tried to subdue the Hussites and followed in command after becoming blind.

Mainz printer who developed a printing system with metal moving types in 15th century Europe. His forty-two-line Bible, made with the participation of Johann Fust and Peter Schöffer, transformed the production of the book.

eventos.descripcion: Marriage links the Burgundian heritage with the Habsburgs and changes the political balance of Western Europe.
The agreement returns Artois and the Franche Condado to the inheritance of Maria de Burgundy, while the Duchy of Burgundy remains in French hands.

eventos.titulo: Symbolic beginning of the Lutheran Reformation
eventos.descripcion: The controversy over indulgences makes Martin Luther the center of a dispute that soon overflows academic debate and questions authority, doctrine and obedience.
Charles V demands Luther to retract. The refusal of the reformer and the political protection of Frederick the Wise transform a theological dispute into a constitutional problem of the Empire.
Imperial forces defeat the French army and capture King Francis I.
Imperial mutiny troops plunder Rome during the Italian Wars.
The agreement legally accepts the coexistence of Catholic and Lutheran territories within the Empire and recognizes that religious unity can no longer be restored by mere imperial imposition.
Charles V progressively splits his domains between the Spanish branch and the Austrian branch of the Habsburgs.
Philip II's naval expedition against England fails after fighting, logistical problems and adverse temporary.
Company of veterans of the Hundred Years War, including John Hawkwood's associate, make the mercenary condotta a decisive force of Italian politics.

eventos.titulo: L'Aquila: fall of Braccio da Montone
eventos.descripcion: The war of L'Aquila destroys the power of Braccio da Montone and accelerates the rise of a new generation of captains, including Francesco Sforza and Niccolò Piccinino.
Carmagnola's execution shows the system's essential tension: states needed great captains, but feared that their private interests would end up imposing on those of the employer.

eventos.titulo: Francesco Sforza marries Bianca Maria Visconti
eventos.descripcion: Marriage introduces a condotiero to the succession of the Duchy of Milan and demonstrates to what extent military force could be transformed into dynastic legitimacy.
Francesco Sforza culminates the most extraordinary career of a condotiero: from mercenary captain to founder of a ducal dynasty.
The peace between Milan and Venice inaugurates an Italian balance that reduces the political space for the great independent captains and favors armies more controlled by the states.
The Venetian defeat of Agnadello shows the condotiers in wars already dominated by large international coalitions and armies of a much larger scale.

eventos.titulo: Leonardo enters the service of the Sforza
eventos.descripcion: Leonardo settled in Milan and for years developed a career at the service of the court of Ludovico Sforza.
Leonardo portrays Cecilia Gallerani, Ludovico Sforza's lover. In 1491 Cecilia will give Ludovico a son, Cesare.
Bianca Giovanna Sforza belonged to the Milanese circle in which Leonardo’s first major court period took shape. A modern minority hypothesis has proposed her as the model for the Mona Lisa.

eventos.titulo: Leonardo in the service of César Borja
eventos.descripcion: Leonardo works as a military engineer for César Borja during his campaigns in central Italy.

eventos.titulo: The story of the Gioconda begins
eventos.descripcion: The traditional and now dominant identification relates the portrait to Lisa Gherardini, wife of Florentine merchant Francesco del Giocondo.
Leonardo returns to Milan under the protection of French governor Charles II d'Amboise.

eventos.titulo: Leonardo in the Rome of the Medici
eventos.descripcion: Leonardo is installed in Rome under the protection of Giuliano de' Medici during the pontificate of Leo X.

eventos.titulo: Francis I calls Leonardo to France
eventos.descripcion: Leonardo moves to France accompanied by Francesco Melzi and enters the orbit of Francis I.
Leonardo dies in France. Gioconda remained with him until his last years and ended up joining the French royal collection.
After the collapse of Hohenstaufen authority, several rival kings dispute an imperial crown whose capacity to impose obedience is greatly weakened.

eventos.titulo: Rodolfo of Habsburg is elected king of Romans
eventos.descripcion: The election of Rodolfo I closes the Great Interregno and places the Habsburgs for the first time at the centre of imperial politics.

eventos.titulo: Marchfeld and the Austrian Habsburg base
eventos.descripcion: The defeat and death of Otakar II allows the consolidation of the Habsburgical appropriation of Austria and Styria, the territorial base of a dynasty that will take generations to monopolize the imperial crown.

The coronation of Frederick III inaugurates an extraordinary dynastic continuity: except for a brief interruption in the eighteenth century, imperial dignity will remain linked to the Habsburgs and then to the Habsburg-Lorraine.
The Worms Diet promotes common mechanisms of justice, public peace and political organization that attempt to make a ruleable empire composed of hundreds of territorial powers.

eventos.titulo: Charles V is elected king of Romans
eventos.descripcion: The succession of Maximilian I makes the imperial election a European competition. Charles brings together the imperial crown with a dynastic heritage that extends from the Netherlands to Spain and America.
In the absence of a male heir, Charles VI attempts to ensure the indivisibility of Habsburg domains and the succession of his future daughter Mary Theresa.

In the midst of the Austrian War of Succession, elector Wittelsbach Charles Albert obtains the imperial crown and demonstrates that dignity remains elective, even after centuries of Habsburg dominance.

eventos.titulo: Francis I opens the Habsburg-Lorraine house
eventos.descripcion: The election of Francisco Esteban returns the crown to the dynastic environment of Maria Teresa and creates the Habsburg-Lorraine line.
Joseph II succeeds his father as emperor and, after 1780, tries to quickly reform the Habsburg domains, repeatedly colliding with territorial and corporate privileges.
The revolution in France upsets the European political balance and makes the fate of Marie Antoinette, sister of Joseph II and Leopold II, an international dynastic problem.

eventos.titulo: Pope Francis II to Revolutionary Europe
eventos.descripcion: Francis II inherits the imperial crown in the midst of revolutionary war. As 1800 arrives, the old Empire still exists, but faces a transformation that will culminate a few years later.

The Greek and Latin edition of Erasmus represents the humanist program of returning to sources and submitting texts to philological examination, a decisive intellectual climate for religious controversies of the sixteenth century.
The confrontation with Johann Eck pushes Luther beyond the question of indulgences: discussion reaches papal authority, councils and the primacy of Scripture.
The Zurich public disputes support Ulrico Zuinglio’s program. The Reformation ceases to be only a Saxon phenomenon and takes its own Swiss path.
Princes and reformist cities protest against the reversal of religious concessions. From this political protest is born the name that will end up identifying Protestant churches.
Philip Melanchthon presents Charles V with a systematic exhibition of Lutheran faith, supported by several princes and cities of the Empire.
The council clarifies Catholic doctrine and approves disciplinary reforms in three major phases, under three pontificates, while the confessional division of Europe becomes permanent.
Charles V defeats the Escaleld League and captures its two great leaders, but military victory fails to restore the religious unity of the Empire.
The final phase of the Council culminates in a programme of doctrinal definition and ecclesiastical reform that will shape the Catholicism of the Modern Age.

The young Florentine chancellery sends Nicholas Machiavelli to negotiate with Caterina Sforza in Forlì. The mission places him before a ruler whose resistance and fall will reappear later in his reflections on fortresses, popular support and power.

The relief army led by John III Sobieski, with Polish, Habsburgenic and Holy Roman Empire forces, breaks the Ottoman siege of Vienna on September 12, 1683. Victory opens a new phase of the war in Hungary and reinforces the rise of the Habsburg monarchy in central Europe.

eventos.titulo: Augustus the Fort gets the crown
eventos.descripcion: The Elector of Saxony converts to Catholicism and succeeds in being elected king. Poland-Lithuania is personally united to Saxony and his election turns the crown back into a European issue.

eventos.titulo: Two elections for a single crown
eventos.descripcion: Estanislao Leszczyński and Augusto III are proclaimed by rival factions. The dispute leads to a European war and shows how far neighbouring powers can condition electoral freedom.

eventos.titulo: May 3 Constitution tries to change the system
eventos.descripcion: The new constitution eliminates the veto liberum and replaces the elective monarchy with an inherited succession foreseen in the house of Saxony. It is the most ambitious attempt to reform the Republic from within.

eventos.titulo: Third partition ends with the Commonwealth
eventos.descripcion: The third partition erases the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth from the political map and forces Stanislaus Augusto to abdicate. The chosen crown experiment ends under pressure from neighbouring monarchies.

The death of Francisco de Anjou makes Enrique de Navarra an alleged heir. Enrique de Guise reorganizes the Catholic League, backed from Spain, to prevent a Protestant from inheriting the French crown.
The death of Frederick II leaves his kingdom of Sicily in the hands of a Hohenstaufen dynasty facing the papacy. Conrad IV inherits the crown, while Manfredo maintains the family position in Italy.

Alfonso V of Aragon defeats the Angevin resistance and enters Naples. For the first time since Vespers, the same monarch controls Aragon, Trinacria and the continental kingdom, although the crowns retain separate identities.

eventos.titulo: France and Aragon are distributed Naples
eventos.descripcion: Louis XII and Ferdinand the Catholic agree to divide the kingdom of Frederick I. Cooperation lasts little: disputes over the boundaries of partition make the former allies enemies.

eventos.titulo: Cerignola: the Great Captain changes the war
eventos.descripcion: The forces of Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba defeat the French in Cerignola. The combined use of infantry, field fortification and firearms consolidates the Aragonese position in southern Italy.
A second great victory of the Grand Captain forces the French forces to withdraw. The balance born of the 1500 cast is definitely broken in favour of Fernando.

eventos.titulo: Ferdinand gathers Naples and Trinacria under his crown
eventos.descripcion: The French defeat leaves Ferdinand the Catholic as king of Naples in addition to Trinacria. The two parts of the former Sicilian monarchy once again share sovereign, although they will continue to be administered as distinct kingdoms.

eventos.titulo: Pius V gets the Holy League
eventos.descripcion: Pius V achieves an agreement between the Hispanic Monarchy, Venice and the Pontifical States. Philip II provides an essential part of the resources and his half-brother Don Juan of Austria receives the supreme command of the allied fleet.

eventos.titulo: Hungarian rebellion opens a door to the Sultan
eventos.descripcion: Imre Thököly leads a Hungarian opposition to the Habsburgs and seeks Ottoman support. The internal conflict of Leopoldo I’s monarchy is mixed with imperial rivalry in central Europe.

eventos.titulo: Leopoldo and Sobieski agree to mutual relief
eventos.descripcion: With papal mediation, Leopold I and John III Sobieski agree on a defensive alliance. If Vienna or Krakow are attacked, the other sovereign must turn to the aid of the ally.

The great Visir Kara Mustafa leads the Ottoman army to Vienna. Leopold leaves the capital and Ernst Rüdiger von Starhemberg organizes the defense while the fortifications suffer weeks of siege and minework.

eventos.titulo: Poles, Imperials and German Princes Gather
eventos.descripcion: Charles V of Lorraine coordinates the imperial forces and joins contingents from Bavaria, Saxony and other territories of the Empire. Sobieski arrives with the Polish army and assumes command of the relief operation.

eventos.titulo: From saving Vienna to going on the offensive
eventos.descripcion: After the victory a new Holy League was formed. Habsburg, Poland and Venice transform an emergency defense into a prolonged war against the Ottoman Empire.
The conquest of Buda shows that Vienna was not an isolated episode. The war begun in 1683 becomes a Habsburgic expansion by Hungary and permanently alters the balance of Central Europe.

eventos.titulo: Frederick II Recovers Jerusalem by Treaty
eventos.descripcion: The Sixth Crusade temporarily returns Jerusalem to free control through negotiation, reinforcing the link of the Jerusalem crown with the Hohenstaufen.

historias.titulo: Burgundy: the Kingdom That Was Not

people.nombre: Frederick I of the Holy Roman Empire
people.resumen: Frederick I, called Barbarossa, was King of the Romans from 1152 and emperor from 1155. A Hohenstaufen, he contested power in Italy and took part in the Third Crusade. He set out overland in 1189 and drowned in the River Saleph on 10 June 1190, before reaching the Holy Land. He was the father of Philip of Swabia.
Duke of Austria from 1358. He commissioned the forged Privilegium maius to raise Austria’s standing, founded the University of Vienna in 1365 and acquired Tyrol.

Federico II, called the Battler, succeeded Leopold VI in Austria and Styria in 1230. Their clashes with nobles, neighbors and the emperor marked their government. He died fighting the Hungarians by the Leitha in 1246, without offspring, and opened a long dispute over the Babenberg heritage.
It consolidated the Přemysl monarchy in Bohemia and favored the growth of cities and internal colonization. His reign coincided with the Mongolian invasion of Central Europe.
Consort of the Hohenstaufen dynasty. Their life was connected with Bohemia.
King of Bohemia who built a powerful Central European domain and gained control of Austria. His defeat and death against Rudolf of Habsburg at Marchfeld changed the Empire’s dynastic balance.
Consort of the Rurikid dynasty. Their life was connected with Bohemia.
Noble of the Árpád dynasty. Their life was connected with Bavaria.
Duke of Bavaria, 1253–1290 (branch). Duke of the Wittelsbach dynasty.

He brought together the crowns of Bohemia and Poland and turned the Argentinian wealth of Kutnah Hora into an support of his power. His dynastic expansion prepared his son's candidacy for his Hungarian throne.
Consort of the Habsburg dynasty. Their life was connected with Bohemia.
Consort of the Piast dynasty. Their life was connected with Bohemia.
The violent death of Wenceslao III extinguished the male line of the Přemysl that ruled Bohemia. His claims about Poland and Hungary show the scope and fragility of that dynastic expansion.
King of Hungary and Bohemia and subsequently emperor. His involvement in the Great Schism, the Hussite Wars and the Council of Constance made him a central figure in fifteenth-century Europe.
Duke of Bavaria, 1290–1312 (branch). Duke of the Wittelsbach dynasty.
Consort of the Habsburg dynasty. Their life was connected with Bavaria.
He was elected King of the Romans as an alternative to candidates from more powerful houses. The electors eventually deposed him, and he died fighting Albert of Habsburg.
His marriage to Elizabeth of Bohemia established the Luxembourgs on the throne in Prague. He campaigned throughout Europe and died at Crécy after losing his sight.
Consort of the Přemyslid dynasty. Their life was connected with Bohemia.
Consort of the Bourbon dynasty. Their life was connected with Bohemia.

people.nombre: Henry VII of the Holy Roman Empire
people.resumen: The first emperor of the House of Luxembourg. He attempted to restore imperial authority in Italy, but his early death left unfinished a project that anticipated his dynasty’s rise.
Consort of the Brabant dynasty. Their life was connected with Germany, Luxembourg.
King of the Romans who began the political rise of the Habsburgs. His victory over Ottokar II enabled his family to establish itself in Austria, the base of its future dynastic power.
Consort of the Hohenberg dynasty. Their life was connected with Germany.
Consort of the Burgundy dynasty. Their life was connected with Germany.
Noble of the Pirovan dynasty. Their life was connected with Milan.
Noble of the Visconti dynasty. Their life was connected with Milan.
Consort of the Borri dynasty. Their life was connected with Milan.
Captain of the people of Milan, 1287–1301. Lord of the Visconti dynasty.
Consort of the Doria dynasty. Their life was connected with Milan.
Noble of the Visconti dynasty. Their life was connected with Milan.
Louis the Strict, Duke of Upper Bavaria and Count Palatine of the Rhine. In 1256 he had his wife Maria of Brabant executed on suspicion of adultery; he was Conradin’s guardian.
Consort of the Habsburg dynasty. Their life was connected with Bavaria.
Consort of the Brabant dynasty. Their life was connected with Bavaria.
Consort of the Přemyslid dynasty. Their life was connected with Austria.
Duke of Austria, 1282–1283 (Co-ruler). Duke of the Habsburg dynasty.
A Wittelsbach emperor whose struggle for the German crown led to a prolonged conflict with the papacy. His reign reflected the political divisions of the fourteenth-century Holy Roman Empire.
Countess of Hainaut, 1345–1356. Consort of the Avesnes dynasty.
Consort of the Piast dynasty. Their life was connected with Germany, Bavaria.
Consort of the Savoy dynasty. Their life was connected with Milan.
Co-ruler of Milan, 1354–1378, of the House of Visconti.
Co-ruler of Milan, 1354–1385, of the House of Visconti.
Consort of the Della Scala dynasty. Their life was connected with Milan.

people.nombre: Frederick II of the Holy Roman Empire
people.resumen: A Hohenstaufen emperor, King of Sicily and Jerusalem, and an exceptional figure in thirteenth-century Mediterranean politics. His conflict with the papacy and his Sicilian court shaped an era.
King of Castile and León, famous for his cultural, legal and scientific programme. His court promoted one of the greatest intellectual undertakings of medieval Europe.

An emperor of the House of Luxembourg and King of Bohemia, he made Prague one of Europe’s leading political and cultural centres. The Golden Bull of 1356 established a lasting framework for imperial elections.
Consort of the Wittelsbach dynasty. Their life was connected with Bohemia, Germany.
Consort of the Piast dynasty. Their life was connected with Bohemia, Holy Roman Empire.
Consort of the Valois dynasty. Their life was connected with Bohemia, Germany.
Consort of the Griffin dynasty. Their life was connected with Bohemia, Holy Roman Empire.
King of Bohemia and King of the Romans, although the electors deposed him from the latter office. The religious and political tensions of his time preceded the Hussite Wars.
He consolidated the Habsburg position in Austria and won the German kingship after defeating Adolf of Nassau. His nephew John assassinated him.
Consort of the Gorizia dynasty. Their life was connected with Germany, Austria.
His government helped consolidate the Habsburgs’ Austrian dominions. The acquisition of Carinthia extended the dynasty’s territorial reach.
A Habsburg duke of Austria who founded the Leopoldian line after dividing the family’s dominions with his brother Albert III in 1379. He died fighting the Swiss Confederates at Sempach in 1386.
Consort of the Visconti dynasty. Their life was connected with Austria, Milan.
Duke of Inner Austria, 1406–1424. Duke of the Habsburg dynasty.

people.nombre: Frederick III of the Holy Roman Empire
people.resumen: A Habsburg emperor whose exceptionally long reign preserved and patiently extended his house’s interests. His son Maximilian’s marriage to Mary of Burgundy transformed the dynasty’s future.
The daughter of King Duarte of Portugal and Leonor of Aragon, married Frederick III and was crowned Empress in Rome in 1452. Mother of Maximilian I, died in 1467.
Habsburg emperor whose marriage policy laid the foundations of his house’s extraordinary dynastic expansion across Europe.
Consort of the Sforza dynasty. Their life was connected with Holy Roman Empire, Milan.
The first Visconti Duke of Milan. Through war, diplomacy and territorial purchases, he built a dominion that aspired to become the leading power in northern Italy.
Consort of the Valois dynasty. Their life was connected with Milan, France.
Consort of the Visconti dynasty. Their life was connected with Milan.
Consort of the Visconti dynasty. Their life was connected with Milan, France.
The last Duke of Milan in the male Visconti line. His death opened a crisis that passed through the Ambrosian Republic before Francesco Sforza’s rise to power.
Noble of the The Maine dynasty. Their life was connected with Milan.
The only daughter of Filippo Maria Visconti, Duke of Milan. Her marriage to the condottiere Francesco Sforza (1441) enabled him to take control of the duchy in 1450.
Count of the Sforza dynasty. Their life was connected with Milan, Naples.
Noble. Their life is linked to Milan.
Consort. Their life was connected with Milan.
Count of the Sforza dynasty. Their life was connected with Milan, Tuscany.
A condottiere who became Duke of Milan after marrying Bianca Maria Visconti. He founded the Sforza dynasty and stabilised the duchy within the Italian balance of power of the mid-fifteenth century.
Consort of the Sforza dynasty. Their life was connected with Milan, Naples.
His Milanese court was noted for its musical patronage and princely ceremonial. He was assassinated in a church in Milan, leaving an underage heir.
Noble. Their life is linked to Milan.
An Italian noblewoman, ruler of Imola and Forlì and one of the best-known figures in the politics of Romagna. She defended her domains vigorously until her defeat by Cesare Borgia.
Consort of the Sforza dynasty. Their life was connected with Milan, Ferrara.
He inherited the Duchy of Milan as a child, while power remained in the hands of his uncle Ludovico. The gap between his title and effective authority shaped the Sforza succession.
Consort of the Trastámara dynasty. Their life was connected with Milan, Naples.
He governed Milan first as his nephew’s guardian and later as duke. His alliance policy encouraged French intervention in Italy, which eventually brought about his downfall.
Consort of the Este dynasty. Their life was connected with Milan, Ferrara.
Noble of the Gallerani dynasty. Their life was connected with Milan.
Noble. Their life is linked to Milan.
Noble of the Sforza dynasty. Their life was connected with Milan.
Count of the Sanseverino dynasty. Their life was connected with Milan, France.
Consort of the Piast dynasty. Their life was connected with Bavaria.
Duke of Bavaria, 1312–1333 (branch). Duke of the Wittelsbach dynasty.
Consort of the Habsburg dynasty. Their life was connected with Bavaria.
His rival election against Louis of Bavaria divided the German kingship. After defeat and imprisonment at Mühldorf, he sought an agreement with his opponent.

He left his ecclesiastical career before succeeding his brother Peter II. With no children of his own, he had to arrange an inheritance contested by the sons and grandsons of Thomas II.
Amadseus's brother, his father, was awarded rights at Piedmont and Flanders ruled his marriage with Juana. He was his father's successor in Savoy County.
Consort of the Fieschi dynasty. Their life was connected with Piedmont, Savoy.

Daughter of Theodore I of Montferrat, married Aimon of Savoy. His descent linked with the emperor Andronikos II and the Aleramici heiress Yolanda, named Irene in Byzantium.

Known as the Green Count, he belonged to the generation that strengthened Savoy’s political and military reach. He was the son of Aymon and Yolanda of Montferrat, bringing together Savoyrd and Palaiologan ancestry.
Consort of the Bourbon dynasty. Their life was connected with Bourbon, Savoy.

The Red Count succeeded his father Amadeo VI and maintained the relationship with the French monarchy. He married Bona of Berry and was the father of Amadeo VIII. His early death left a child heir and opened a struggle for regency between the mother and the new count's grandmother.
Consort of the Valois dynasty. Their life was connected with France, Savoy.
He inherited as a child and became the first duke of Savoy in 1416. The House of Savoy continued to rule its territories with ducal rank.
Consort of the Valois-Burgundy dynasty. Their life was connected with Burgundy, Savoy.

The daughter of King Jano of Cyprus, married Louis of Savoy and brought a direct connection to the Lusignan to the Alpine court. His numerous offspring linked with France, Milan and the Cypriot succession itself.
Duke of Savoy from 1465, in fragile health because of epilepsy. His wife Yolande of France exercised government in practice. He was beatified for his piety.

He inherited the duchy from his brother Philibert I. His marriage to Blanche of Montferrat strengthened Savoy’s expectations of the Palaeologan inheritance, while intervention in Saluzzo brought him into conflict with French interests.

Son of Louis and Anne of Cyprus, he became duke after his brother Amadeus IX’s male descendants died out. His brief government preceded those of his sons Philibert II and Charles III, born from different marriages.
Consort of the Bourbon dynasty. Their life was connected with Bourbon, Savoy.

Son of Emmanuel Philibert, he governed amid the rivalry between France and the Spanish monarchy. His marriage to Catherine Michelle connected him with Philip II.

Princess of Carignano of the Bourbon-Condé dynasty. Their life was connected with France, Savoy.

Son of Thomas Francis of Savoy-Carignano, he inherited from his mother the county of Soissons and served as a general in the armies of Louis XIV. He married Olympia Mancini, niece of Mazarino, and was the father of Prince Eugene.

A prince of the house of Savoy-Carignano raised at the court of Louis XIV, he entered Habsburg service in 1683 and became the Empire’s leading general. He defeated the Ottomans at Zenta (1697) and Belgrade (1717) and, alongside Marlborough, defeated France at Blenheim, Oudenarde and Malplaquet during the War of the Spanish Succession.

King of Sardinia and duke of Savoy who continued his dynasty’s territorial expansion in northern Italy. He played an active role in the major European wars of the eighteenth century.

King of Sardinia and duke of Savoy from 1773. War with Revolutionary France cost him Savoy and Nice, ceded under the Armistice of Cherasco in 1796.

people.nombre: Catherine of Brandenburg, Princess of Transylvania
people.resumen: Elected successor to her husband Gabriel Bethlen, he briefly ruled in his own right. His resignation in 1630 shows the limits that the staments and factions imposed on the principality power; it was not just a consort.

Bernabò Visconti’s daughter married Peter II to strengthen relations between Milan and Cyprus. Their only daughter died young. After being widowed, she returned to Italy. The Duchess of Orléans was another member of the Visconti family named Valentina.

people.nombre: Louis of Savoy, King of Cyprus
people.resumen: Son of Louis of Savoy and Anne of Cyprus, he married his cousin Charlotte. His royal dignity derived from that marriage and subsequently became a claim maintained in exile. His father Louis held the Duchy of Savoy.

people.nombre: Gaston of Foix, Duke of Nemours
people.resumen: The son of John of Foix and Mary of Orleans, he was nephew of Louis XII and brother of Germana of Foix. He led French forces during the wars in Italy and died in the battle of Ravenna in 1512. His career brings together the Pirenaic connections of the Foix and military service to the French monarchy.

Erik of Pomerania’s sister married John of the Palatinate-Neumarkt, of the House of Wittelsbach. Their son Christopher was elected in each of the three Nordic kingdoms after Erik’s fall. The kinship shows dynastic continuity, although Christopher’s accession depended on separate elections.

The son of the king of Romans Rupiro and a member of the house of Wittelsbach. His marriage with Catherine of Pomerania linked his palatine branch with Eric of pomerania. He was the father of Christopher of Bavaria, his choice in the Scandinavian kingdoms and his association beyond German territories.

Daughter of William VIII of Montferrat, married Charles I of Savoy. After the death of the Duke, he took over the regency of his son Carlos Juan Amadeo and defended his authority before the relatives of the house.
Son of Charles I and Blanche of Montferrat, he inherited Savoy before his first birthday. His mother exercised the regency.

people.nombre: Juana de Savoy, Marquesa de Montferrat
people.resumen: The daughter of Amadeus VII and Bona de Berry married John Jacobo of Montferrat. He was the mother of William VIII, Boniface III and Elizabeth, and his wife Ludovicus I of Saluzzo.
He inherited his father's electoral dignity in 1410. The family division left separate palatines branches and since 1435 a guardianship council exercised the government for his illness.
Son of Louis III, he agreed to be a minor. A tutelar council administered the Kurpfalz until it personally assumed the government in 1442.
Brother of Louis IV, assumed electoral dignity in 1449. His access opened a tutelage and a successor arrangement whose final beneficiary was his nephew Philip.
The Nephew of Federico I, happened in the electoral dignity in 1476. His offspring continued the ruling line of the Kurpfalz during the first half of the 16th century.
Elector of the Palatinate since 1508. His brother Frederick II has succeeded; none of these governments must be confused with the collateral branches of Pfalz- Neuburg.
Brother and successor of Louis V, he ruled the electoral palatinate until 1556. He was followed by Otto Henry, from the branch of Neuburg.

He ruled with his brother Philip from 1522 and after his solo. "By inherited in 1556 his palatine electoral dignity remained separate from both principalities and his father gave up his father's Wolfgang from Zweibrücken in 1557.
Elector since 1559, he has driven Calvinism in the Palatinate. His son Louis VI changed the confessional policy again.
He succeeded Frederick III in 1576 and returned to Lutheranism. His son Frederick IV was younger when he died in 1583; the government was under guardianship until 1592.

The son of Frederick V and Elizabeth Estuardo, he was reinstated as elector for the Peace of Westphalia in 1648. He recovered a reduced Palatinate: Bavaria preserved the High Palatinate and the old electoral dignity.
He succeeded his father Charles Louis in 1680. He died without an heir in 1685, so the electoral dignity passed to the Palatinate-Neuburg branch.

He inherited Jülich and Berg of Wolfgang William in 1653 and happened in the Palatinate of the election in 1685. The coincidence in one person did not automatically merge the Renan duchys with the Kurpfalz.

Elector of Bavaria, 1799–1806. Elector of the Wittelsbach dynasty.

Duke of Styria and, since 1198, also from Austria, Leopold VI of Babenberg combined the expansion of his heritage with support for monasteries and cities. He participated in the crusades and measured between Frederick II and the papacy. He died in San Germano in 1230 and was succeeded by his son Federico.
Co-ruler of Milan, 1339–1349, of the House of Visconti.
Co-ruler of Milan, 1339–1354, of the House of Visconti.

A preacher and teacher at the University of Prague who advocated reform of the Church and criticised the sale of indulgences. He was condemned for heresy and executed at the Council of Constance in 1415. His memory gave its name to the Hussite movement.

A commander in the Hussite Wars, distinguished by his troops’ discipline and their use of fortified wagons. He led campaigns against armies seeking to subdue the Hussites and continued in command after becoming blind.

A printer from Mainz who developed a system of printing with movable metal type in fifteenth-century Europe. His forty-two-line Bible, produced with Johann Fust and Peter Schöffer, transformed book production.

name: Brabant
summary: Brabant was a duchy with institutions and succession of his own. Henry IV's resignation in 1267 brought the government to his brother John I, whose offspring linked with England, Évreux and Flanders. When John III died in 1355, his daughter Joan defended the duchy against the claims of his sister Margarita's line. La Joyeuse Entrée of 1356 expressed commitments of the ducal power with the territory. The inheritance passed in 1406 to Antonio de Burgundy and then to his children; only in 1430 it reached his cousin Philip the Good. That sequence allows to understand the incorporation to Burgundy without making the previous Brabantinean story disappear.

uniones.titulo: The Burgundian inheritance, feuded to feud
uniones.resumen: Marriage, succession, purchase, renunciation and conquest gathered different legal fiefdoms. The map must follow each effective government, not paint all domains since the ducal investiture.
uniones.instituciones: Dijon's duchy was a French fief; the Franche Condado, an imperial fiefdom. Nevers and Rethel followed a smaller branch. After 1477, France took the duchy; the claims of Mary and her heirs do not amount to possession.

Louis de Male, Count of Flanders since 1346. Faced with the Flemish cities, his daughter Margarita brought Flanders to the Dukes of Burgundy.

Duke of Burgundy and protagonist of the French civil war. He ordered the murder of Louis of Orleans and ended up murdered in Montereau, feeding the Borgonian alliance with England.

The son of Philip the Bold and Margaret of Flanders, inherited Brabant and Limburg in 1406. The connection came from the brabanon ancestry of his mother. He died in Azincourt; his sons John IV and Philip of Saint-Pol later ruled before the inheritance of Philip the Good.
Count of Nevers, 1404–1415. Count of the Valois-Borgogna dynasty.

Duke of Burgundy and builder of a powerful territorial state between France and the Empire. His court was one of the brightest in 15th century Europe.

personas.resumen: He inherited Hainaut, Holland and Zeeland from his father and defended his rights against John of Bavaria and Philip the Good. Their marriages were part of that political struggle. Delft's agreement of 1428 restricted his power and the 1433 cession incorporated the counties into the Burgundian heritage.
Duke of Burgundy and builder of a powerful territorial state between France and the Empire. His court was one of the brightest in 15th century Europe.

etapas.texto: Charles the Temerary died, Mary retained the Netherlands; France took the duchy and contested Artois and the Franche Condado.

personas.resumen: Last Grand Duke Valois of Burgundy. He died before Nancy in 1477; the French Crown incorporated the duchy, while his daughter Mary inherited rights over the Netherlands and the Franche Condado. The inheritance was disputed and did not remain as a united state.

Heir to Charles the Temerary since 1477 and Duchess titular of Burgundy. His marriage to Maximilian of Habsburg linked that house to the Netherlands of Burgundy. The dispute with France over the duchy, the Franche Condado and Artois prevents presenting all the inheritance as territory that ruled without interruption.
Emperor Habsburg whose marriage policy laid the foundations for the extraordinary dynastic expansion of his house throughout Europe.

etapas.texto: Artois and the Franche Condado returned to the house of Austria; Philip I and Charles V transmitted them to the Netherlands.

personas.resumen: The son of Maria de Burgundy and Maximilian of Habsburg, he inherited the Netherlands and, after Senlis (1493), the Franche Condado and Artois. He preserved the dignity of Duke of Burgundy, although the duchy was under the French Crown. His marriage to Juana I took him to Castile and transmitted heritages other than Charles V.

Emperor of the Holy Roman Empire and sovereign of a composite monarchy that reached the Iberian peninsula, Italy, the Netherlands and America. Philip I inherited the Franche Condado, Artois, Namur and Luxembourg, as well as other Dutch territories. He later incorporated Frisia, Utrecht, Overijssel, Drente, Groningen and Güeldres in a staggered form, between 1524 and 1543. He preserved the ducal dignity of Burgundy, but did not rule the Duchy incorporated into France. Since 1535 he kept Milan under imperial control; the investiture and subsequent possession of Philip II must be distinguished from that government.

translatedSource.resumen: Brabant was a duchy with institutions and succession of his own. Henry IV's resignation in 1267 brought the government to his brother John I, whose offspring linked with England, Évreux and Flanders. When John III died in 1355, his daughter Joan defended the duchy against the claims of his sister Margarita's line. La Joyeuse Entrée of 1356 expressed commitments of the ducal power with the territory. The inheritance passed in 1406 to Antonio de Burgundy and then to his children; only in 1430 it reached his cousin Philip the Good. That sequence allows to understand the incorporation to Burgundy without making the previous Brabantinean story disappear.

eventos.descripcion: Francis II inherits the imperial crown in the midst of revolutionary war. As 1800 arrives, the old Empire still exists, but faces a transformation that will culminate a few years later.
Philip Melanchthon presents Charles V with a systematic exhibition of Lutheran faith, supported by several princes and cities of the Empire.
Charles V defeats the Escaleld League and captures its two great leaders, but military victory fails to restore the religious unity of the Empire.

The death of Francisco de Anjou makes Enrique de Navarra an alleged heir. Enrique de Guise reorganizes the Catholic League, backed from Spain, to prevent a Protestant from inheriting the French crown.

eventos.titulo: Pius V gets the Holy League
eventos.descripcion: Pius V achieves an agreement between the Hispanic Monarchy, Venice and the Pontifical States. Philip II provides an essential part of the resources and his half-brother Don Juan of Austria receives the supreme command of the allied fleet.
